description: We are a team from IEEE Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala Section, motivated by innovation and the development of ideas by all students and professionals in this country.
summary:
We built a public web tool, inspired by the WiseView blink comparator used by Backyard Worlds, that lets anyone see how a patch of sky changes in SPHEREx data. A user enters coordinates or picks a known target (Barnard’s Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, R Draconis). A Python FastAPI backend queries NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive for SPHEREx observations covering that position, requests cutouts of each epoch, and converts the FITS files into contrast-stretched images. The browser plays them as a short time-lapse, blinks between any two epochs, and shows the field in context with Aladin Lite. Objects that move, like high proper-motion stars and nearby brown dwarfs, or that change brightness, like variable stars, stand out at a glance.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared bands, producing far more images than scientists can inspect by eye. Turning archive files into a simple flip-book lowers the barrier so students and citizen scientists can help spot moving and changing objects, including cold, faint ones that could hint at undiscovered worlds.
details:
What it does. Our tool is a web-based “blink comparator” for NASA’s SPHEREx mission. A user types sky coordinates (RA/Dec) or picks one of the challenge’s test targets: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. The tool then shows every SPHEREx observation of that spot as a short time-lapse. The user can play the sequence, scrub through epochs with a slider, or blink between any two epochs. Anything that moved or changed brightness jumps out immediately, while fixed background stars stay still. An Aladin Lite panel shows the surrounding sky for context.

How it works. A Python FastAPI backend queries NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) for SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images covering the requested position. It tries the TAP service (spherex.obscore) first and falls back to SIA. For each epoch it requests a small cutout through IRSA’s cutout service and opens the multi-extension FITS file with Astropy. It takes the image extension and applies a zscale + asinh stretch so faint sources stay visible, then returns a PNG to the browser. The frontend is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step, so it is easy to host and easy for others to modify. Because IRSA can be slow under heavy load, the tool also has an offline demo mode that generates simulated sequences. A banner on screen labels it as simulated, so we never pass it off as real data.

Benefits and impact. SPHEREx images the entire sky every six months in 102 infrared bands, which is far more data than scientists can inspect by eye. Projects like Backyard Worlds have shown that volunteers looking at blinking images can find nearby brown dwarfs that automated searches missed. Our goal is to bring that same approach to SPHEREx: no software installation and no knowledge of FITS files, just coordinates in and a moving picture out. This makes SPHEREx data usable for students, teachers and citizen scientists, and it gives researchers a quick way to check a candidate.

Creativity. Instead of building another archive search page, we turned archive files into a flip-book, the same technique astronomers used to discover Pluto. The stretch is tuned for infrared images with faint sources, and the tool works for any position on the sky, not only for preset objects.

Factors we considered. Reliability during a live demo (timeouts, fallbacks, clear error messages, an offline mode). Honesty about data (simulated images are always labeled). Accessibility (works in any browser and loads only small cutouts instead of full images). Accuracy of target positions (Barnard’s Star has a high proper motion, so we documented the coordinate epoch). Keeping the architecture simple enough to extend later with epoch subtraction, band selection and catalog overlays.

Tools. Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Astropy, NumPy, Pillow, Requests, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Aladin Lite, Git/GitHub. Part of the code and documentation was written with the help of AI coding assistants; the team made the design decisions, validated the data and did the final review.
